questions.q: In a GitOps pipeline, what is the CI pipeline's actual last action before a change reaches production, after build/test/push-image?
options: Running kubectl apply directly against the production cluster
Committing a manifest change (such as a bumped image tag) to the Git repo and opening a pull request
Deleting the previous production deployment
SSHing into a cluster node to restart the kubelet
questions.explain: In GitOps, CI's final act is to touch Git, not the cluster — it updates the manifest (e.g. the image tag) and opens a PR; an in-cluster agent is what performs the actual deployment from there.

questions.q: According to the stage-by-stage comparison in this lesson, what detects configuration drift in a plain CI/CD pipeline that just runs kubectl apply?
options: Nothing does — it's invisible until someone happens to notice unexpected cluster behavior
The CI pipeline automatically re-applies manifests every hour
Kubernetes itself rejects any manual kubectl command outright
A built-in kubectl flag that blocks out-of-band changes
questions.explain: Plain CI/CD has no continuous reconciliation loop watching for drift; a manual change can sit unnoticed until it causes a visible problem, unlike GitOps's continuous reconciliation.

questions.q: How does environment promotion (staging to production) typically work in a GitOps model, versus a plain CI/CD pipeline?
options: GitOps promotion requires rebuilding the container image from scratch for each environment
Both models promote identically, by re-running the same pipeline against a different kubectl context
Plain CI/CD promotion is always a pull request; GitOps promotion is always a pipeline parameter
GitOps promotion is a Git operation — a pull request that copies a change from the staging overlay into the production overlay — rather than re-running a pipeline against a different target
questions.explain: In GitOps, promotion means opening a PR that merges a change already proven in the staging overlay into the production overlay, giving reviewers a literal diff of what's about to run in production.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say that a team which keeps YAML in Git but still lets CI run kubectl apply directly against the cluster has NOT adopted GitOps?
options: Because YAML manifests are not a valid way to describe Kubernetes resources
Because that team has kept the push model and just moved the files into a repo, without satisfying the Pulled Automatically or Continuously Reconciled principles
Because Git cannot store files larger than 100 KB
Because kubectl apply is incompatible with any version of Kubernetes released after 1.20
questions.explain: Storing manifests in Git only satisfies the Declarative and Versioned and Immutable principles; without a pull-based in-cluster agent and continuous reconciliation, the pipeline is still push-based CI/CD with its YAML relocated, not GitOps.

questions.q: In the GitOps model described in this lesson, how does rollback typically work compared to plain CI/CD?
options: GitOps rollback requires manually guessing at the cluster's prior kubectl state, same as plain CI/CD
Rollback is identical in both models and requires rebuilding from source control history
GitOps rollback is a git revert, which the in-cluster agent then automatically re-applies; plain CI/CD rollback means re-running a previous pipeline execution or guessing at prior kubectl state
Rollback is not possible in either model once a deployment has shipped
questions.explain: A git revert creates a new commit undoing a bad change, and the GitOps agent's reconciliation loop automatically re-applies that reverted state — a much more reliable path than re-running an old pipeline execution.
